assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators opened a new class of quantum matter, with protected edge and surface states defined by band topology rather than symmetry breaking. It is a clear, verified discovery in materials, and electronic-structure theory (band inversion, spin-orbit coupling) predicts it quantitatively, which is the style of result I value most.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal; Molenkamp's group delivered the HgTe/CdTe measurement of edge transport that confirmed it. That is a natural theory plus experiment trio. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction), Fu, Hasan and others also contributed, so the boundary of credit is arguable, but this configuration is defensible from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in many materials and by ARPES and transport over roughly two decades; the interpretation is stable and the field is mature. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) is not among the supplied names, so the allocation is contested.
I am recalling the history from memory and have not verified the detailed priority claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene shows how a moire superlattice yields flat bands and correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable carbon system. It created the field of moire quantum matter and is exactly the kind of surprise from a two-dimensional material that quantum mechanics keeps delivering.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle from a continuum model; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity. Theory and experiment are cleanly paired. Cao and Fatemi, who did the first measurements, and Dean, Kim and Young are not in the supplied credit, which leaves a fair-credit problem.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and extended to other moire systems, but the origin of the superconductivity is still debated. Eight years after the discovery, recognition would be fast but defensible.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved, so the physical interpretation is incomplete.
Junior experimental contributors are not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gave the first controlled and general nonperturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, explaining the Mott transition and correlated metals and enabling realistic materials calculations when combined with DFT (DFT+DMFT). I know its value in practice from my own field, where it is routinely tested against spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar built the mapping to an impurity problem, and Kotliar developed the DFT+DMFT link. Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt are a sound trio, though Metzner's and Müller-Hartmann's early role and Rozenberg's contribution are not in the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Mature, widely used over three decades, with experimental checks in transition-metal oxides and cuprates, though quantitative predictions depend on approximations (impurity solvers, double counting).
uncertainties: Systematic errors in DFT+DMFT make it less of a single verified discovery than a method.
Metzner's priority is not available in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large tunnel magnetoresistance at room temperature in magnetic tunnel junctions, and later giant TMR in MgO junctions, underlies read heads and MRAM. It is a quantum-mechanical spin-dependent tunnelling effect with large practical consequences, a natural successor to GMR from 2007.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently demonstrated room-temperature TMR in 1995. Parkin (and Yuasa) developed the MgO giant TMR in 2004. Butler and Mathon predicted coherent tunnelling from first principles, a theory contribution I know well, and it is not in the supplied names; Yuasa also is absent. The three-person configuration is plausible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and commercial, with a long period of independent confirmation. Timing is late rather than premature, which raises an issue of dilution of the GMR precedent.
uncertainties: Credit for MgO giant TMR (Parkin, Yuasa, Butler, Mathon) is divided between several groups.
Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize may be argued against.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock reached fractional uncertainties around 1e-18, far beyond the cesium standard, and is poised to redefine the second and test fundamental constants. It combines the magic-wavelength idea with ultra-stable lasers and is a clean, measurable achievement.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength trapping concept and realised the first strontium lattice clock; Ye drove the precision and many-body (spin-exchange, Fermi-degenerate) developments. A two-person award is clean, though Ye's work also relates to the frequency comb prize of 2005.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many independent labs worldwide, and ready for the redefinition of the SI second. Timing is good.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier precision-measurement prizes (2005, 2012) could be argued.
The ion-clock line of work (Wineland) is not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopy of single sites. They provide a clean experimental platform for the correlated-electron physics I study theoretically.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition and developed microscopy. Credit is reasonably clean. Hänsch and Jaksch, and others also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Mature and heavily confirmed, but the most striking claims for solving open fermionic Hubbard problems are still developing.
uncertainties: Whether simulators have answered questions that classical computation could not remains open.
Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 AMO prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of intrinsic ferromagnetism in monolayer CrI3 and bilayer Cr2Ge2Te6 showed that long-range magnetic order survives in two dimensions thanks to anisotropy, overturning a naive reading of the Mermin-Wagner theorem. It is a magnetism discovery with direct links to spin-wave and exchange theory, and I know the first-principles side.
assessment.attribution: The two 2017 papers came from Xu's group (CrI3) and Zhang's group (Cr2Ge2Te6). Jarillo-Herrero's role was in later work and is less decisive, so I would favour Xu and Zhang; I choose this trio only if the credited three are needed, otherwise two.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced widely and developed into a van der Waals magnet field, but applications are still immature and it is a young field, so the recognition is probably premature.
uncertainties: Premature compared with other condensed-matter candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultrasoft pseudopotentials and the projector augmented-wave method made plane-wave DFT efficient and accurate for transition metals and magnets, underlying most of today's computational materials work and the reproducibility of results across codes. I weigh this carefully as it is my own field and I may be biased.
assessment.attribution: Vanderbilt invented ultrasoft pseudopotentials, Blöchl the PAW method, and Kresse and Joubert built the practical PAW implementation in VASP. Credit is defensible, though Hamann, Troullier and Martins and others are not credited, and the 1998 chemistry prize already recognised DFT.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and validated against experiment, including the 2016 reproducibility benchmark. The question is whether a methods and software contribution is a physics discovery.
uncertainties: A computational method may be seen as outside the intent of a physics discovery prize.
Potential perceived bias because it is close to my own research.
